about: Text the vendored Summa (sources/summa/summa.xml, CCEL) lost, restored from an existing English edition (corpus-cleanup 1.7; R7, docs/research/R7-summa-structure.md, section 6; Decision log 'The Summa against an independent edition (R7)' and 'Summa text lost inside a paragraph (1.7, R7 question 2)'). TheoCorpus makes no translation of its own: every text here is an edition's printed words, read from the archive.org scan named in 'editions' (the OCR text is vendored at sources/summa/<archive>/) and proofread against the page image. References inside the text are written as CCEL writes them elsewhere in the same translation ('(De Anima iii, 11)', '(Q[72], A[5], ad 1)'), so the adapter expands them the same way. 'units' are whole units, each emitted as its own passage after the paragraph 'after', anchored '<article>/recovered-<n>' (2.1). 'in_place' restores words lost inside a paragraph CCEL kept, or a word it garbled (III q.7 a.5's "a[9]" for "as"): 'find' occurs exactly once in that paragraph's text and is replaced by 'replace'; the passage keeps its anchor and ID (D1), and 'parts' opens a further part inside the paragraph, as in summa_corrections.json.

units.text: Further, the Philosopher says (De Gener. Animal. ii, 3) that the embryo is an animal before it is a man. But this would be impossible if the essence of the sensitive soul were the same as that of the intellectual soul; for an animal is such by its sensitive soul, while a man is a man by the intellectual soul. Therefore in man the essence of the sensitive soul is not the same as the essence of the intellectual soul.

As the Philosopher says (De Anima iii, 11), a universal opinion does not move except by means of a particular opinion; and in like manner the higher appetite moves by means of the lower: and therefore there are not two distinct motive powers following the intellect and the sense.

Further, if the soul as soon as separated gained knowledge of all natural things, the efforts of men to know would be vain and profitless. But this would be unreasonable. Therefore the separated soul does not know all natural things.
Augustine is speaking of the knowledge of that truth which is not the very Essence of goodness.

Hatred would never overcome love, were it not for the greater love to which that hatred corresponds. Thus man loves himself, more than he loves his friend, and because he loves himself, his friend is hateful to him, if he oppose him.
The reason why we act with greater insistence in repelling what is hateful, is because we feel hatred more keenly.

On the contrary, Things that differ infinitely are not changed into one another. Now venial and mortal sin differ infinitely, as is evident from what has been said above (Q[72], A[5], ad 1; Q[87], A[5], ad 1). Therefore a venial sin cannot become mortal.
S. Gregory says: "The active life precedes the contemplative in the order of time, for from good works a man passes to contemplation."
